chapter_sections.label: DEFINITION:
chapter_sections.text: Sound is a form of energy produced by vibrating objects. It travels through a medium (solid, liquid or gas) and creates the sensation of hearing.

chapter_sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Sound is produced by vibrating bodies.
Sound cannot travel through vacuum.
Sound travels through solids, liquids and gases (mediums).
The human ear detects sound through the vibration of the eardrum.
Sound has properties: amplitude, frequency, time period, loudness, and pitch.
Unpleasant sounds are called noise; pleasing sounds are called music.
Excessive or unwanted sound in the environment is called noise pollution.

items.question: What is sound? How is it produced?
items.answer:
Sound is a form of energy produced by vibrating objects.
When a body vibrates (moves to and fro), it produces sound.
Example: When we strike a plate, it vibrates and produces sound.
When it stops vibrating, sound stops.

items.question: What is vibration?
items.answer:
The to and fro or back and forth motion of an object is called vibration.
This motion is also called oscillatory motion.
Example: A plucked rubber band vibrates and produces sound.

items.question: What are the two properties of sound? Define each.
items.answer:
The two important properties of sound are amplitude and frequency.
AMPLITUDE: The maximum displacement of a vibrating object from its rest position is called amplitude. Larger amplitude means louder sound.
FREQUENCY: The number of oscillations (vibrations) per second is called frequency. Higher frequency means higher pitch or shriller sound.

items.question: What is meant by audible and inaudible sounds? Give the audible range for humans.
items.answer:
AUDIBLE SOUNDS: Sounds that can be detected by the human ear are called audible sounds.
INAUDIBLE SOUNDS: Sounds that cannot be detected by the human ear are called inaudible sounds.
For human beings, the audible frequency range is roughly from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Sounds below 20 Hz and above 20,000 Hz are inaudible to humans.
Some animals like dogs can hear sounds above 20,000 Hz.

items.question: Explain how sound is produced and heard by human beings.
items.answer:
PRODUCTION OF SOUND IN HUMANS:
Sound is produced by the voice box (larynx) in humans.
The larynx is present at the upper end of the windpipe.
Two vocal cords are stretched across the larynx with a narrow slit between them.
When air from the lungs is forced through this slit, the vocal cords vibrate and produce sound.
Muscles attached to vocal cords can make them tight or loose, changing the quality of voice.
Tight and thin vocal cords produce a different voice compared to loose and thick ones.
HEARING SOUND:
The outer ear collects sound and sends it down the ear canal.
At the end of the ear canal is a thin stretched membrane called the eardrum.
Sound vibrations cause the eardrum to vibrate.
These vibrations are sent to the inner ear, which sends signals to the brain.
That is how we hear sound.

items.question: What is noise pollution? What are its causes, harms and measures to control it?
items.answer:
NOISE POLLUTION: The presence of excessive or unwanted sounds in the environment is called noise pollution.
CAUSES: Vehicles, explosions (bursting of crackers), machines, loudspeakers, television and radio at high volumes, kitchen appliances, desert coolers, air conditioners.
HARMS: Lack of sleep, hypertension (high blood pressure), anxiety, many health disorders, temporary or permanent impairment of hearing.
MEASURES TO CONTROL:
- Silencing devices must be installed in aircraft engines, vehicles, industrial machines and home appliances.
- All noisy operations must be conducted away from residential areas.
- Noise-producing industries should be set up far from residential areas.
- Use of automobile horns should be minimised.
- TV and music systems should be run at low volumes.
- Trees must be planted along roads and around buildings to cut down noise levels.

items.question: Describe the structure and function of the human ear. What is the role of the eardrum?
items.answer:
STRUCTURE OF HUMAN EAR:
The outer part of the ear is shaped like a funnel.
Sound enters the ear and travels down a canal.
At the end of the canal is a thin stretched membrane called the EARDRUM (tympanic membrane).
Inside the ear is the inner ear, which receives signals from the eardrum.
FUNCTION:
The funnel-shaped outer ear collects sound from the surroundings.
Sound travels through the ear canal and strikes the eardrum.
Sound vibrations cause the eardrum to vibrate.
The eardrum sends these vibrations to the inner ear.
The inner ear then sends signals to the brain, producing the sensation of hearing.
ROLE OF EARDRUM:
The eardrum acts like a stretched rubber sheet.
It vibrates when sound waves strike it.
It converts sound energy into mechanical vibrations.
These vibrations are transmitted to the inner ear and then to the brain.
IMPORTANT NOTE: We must NEVER put a sharp or hard object into our ear as it can damage the eardrum. A damaged eardrum can impair hearing.

topics.topic_name: SOUND IS PRODUCED BY A VIBRATING BODY

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: Any vibrating object produces sound. Vibration is the to and fro or back and forth motion of an object. This is also called oscillatory motion.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Sound is produced whenever a body vibrates.
When vibration stops, sound production also stops.
Vibrations may be visible (like a stretched rubber band) or invisible (like a tuning fork).
In most cases, amplitude of vibration is too small to see, but we can feel it.
Different musical instruments have different vibrating parts that produce sound.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.1:
sections.aim: To observe that a vibrating object produces sound.
procedure: 1. Hang a metal plate so that it does not touch any wall.
2. Strike it with a stick. Do you hear a sound?
3. Touch the plate or pan gently with your finger. Do you feel vibrations?
4. Strike the plate again and hold it tightly with your hands immediately after striking.
5. Do you still hear the sound? Touch the plate after it stops producing sound.
sections.observation: The plate vibrates and produces sound when struck. When held tightly, vibration stops and sound stops too.
sections.conclusion: A vibrating object produces sound. Sound stops when vibration stops.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.2:
sections.aim: To observe that a plucked rubber band vibrates and produces sound.
sections.materials: Rubber band, pencil box (longer side), two pencils.
procedure: 1. Put a rubber band around the longer side of a pencil box.
2. Insert two pencils between the box and the stretched rubber band.
3. Pluck the rubber band somewhere in the middle.
sections.observation: A sound is heard and the rubber band vibrates when plucked. When it stops vibrating, sound stops.
sections.conclusion: A plucked, vibrating rubber band produces sound.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.3:
sections.aim: To observe that a vibrating object produces sound and link sound with vibrations.
procedure: 1. Take a metal dish. Pour water in it.
2. Strike the dish at its edge with a spoon.
3. Do you hear a sound? Again strike the dish and then touch it.
4. Strike the dish again. Look at the surface of water.
sections.observation: Sound is heard when dish is struck. Water surface shows waves. When the dish is touched and vibration stops, sound stops too.
sections.conclusion: Vibrating objects produce sound. Sound is connected with vibrations of a body.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.4:
sections.aim: To identify the vibrating part of a musical instrument (ektara).
sections.materials: Hollow coconut shell (or earthen pot), thin stick.
procedure: 1. Make an ektara using a hollow coconut shell or earthen pot.
2. Play this instrument and identify the vibrating part.
sections.observation: When the string of the ektara is plucked, it vibrates and produces sound.
sections.conclusion: In a musical instrument, the vibrating part produces sound.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.5:
sections.aim: To make a jaltrang (musical instrument using bowls).
sections.materials: 6 to 8 bowls or tumblers, water, pencil.
procedure: 1. Take 6-8 bowls or tumblers. Fill them with water up to different levels, increasing gradually.
2. Take a pencil and strike all the bowls in succession.
sections.observation: Each bowl produces a different pleasant sound. This is the jaltrang.
sections.conclusion: Different amounts of water in bowls cause different vibrations, producing different sounds.

items.question: What happens to sound when a vibrating body is stopped?
items.answer:
When a vibrating body is stopped (held tightly), its vibrations stop.
As vibration stops, sound production also stops immediately.
This shows that sound is produced only as long as the body vibrates.

items.question: Name any two musical instruments and their vibrating parts.
items.answer:
Veena: the stretched string vibrates to produce sound.
Tabla: the stretched membrane (skin) vibrates to produce sound.
(Other examples: Flute - column of air, Harmonium - metal reeds)

items.question: How would you show that a vibrating object produces sound? Describe an activity.
items.answer: ACTIVITY: Take a metal plate and hang it so it does not touch any wall. Strike it with a stick - you hear a sound. Touch the plate gently - you feel vibrations. Strike the plate again and hold it tightly with your hands immediately after striking. The sound stops at once. Touch the plate - no vibration. This proves that sound is produced by a vibrating object and stops when vibration stops.

items.question: What is oscillatory motion? Give examples of vibrating bodies in musical instruments.
items.answer:
The to and fro or back and forth motion of an object is called vibration. This motion is also called oscillatory motion.
Examples of vibrating parts in musical instruments:
- Veena: stretched string
- Tabla: stretched membrane
- Flute: air column inside the tube
When these parts are made to vibrate, they produce sound.

items.question: Explain with examples how sound is produced by different musical instruments. What is the role of vibration?
items.answer:
Sound is produced whenever an object vibrates. Different musical instruments use different parts to vibrate:
STRING INSTRUMENTS (like Veena, Sitar): When a string is plucked, it vibrates. The vibrating string produces sound. When plucking stops, vibration stops and sound stops.
MEMBRANE INSTRUMENTS (like Tabla, Dholak): When the stretched membrane (skin) is struck, it vibrates and produces sound.
WIND INSTRUMENTS (like Flute): When air is blown through the tube, the air column inside vibrates and produces sound.
PERCUSSION INSTRUMENTS (like Ghatam, Manjira): When struck, the whole body vibrates and produces sound.
ROLE OF VIBRATION: In all musical instruments, the source of sound is always a vibrating part. When the vibration is forced to stop (by touching or holding), sound stops immediately. This confirms that vibration is essential for sound production.

sections.text: Sound is produced by the VOICE BOX or the LARYNX in human beings. It is located at the upper end of the windpipe.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The larynx (voice box) is the organ that produces sound in humans.
Two VOCAL CORDS are stretched across the larynx with a narrow slit between them.
When lungs force air through the slit, the vocal cords vibrate and produce sound.
Muscles can make vocal cords tight (thin) or loose (thick), changing voice quality.
Tight and thin vocal cords produce higher-frequency sound (shriller voice).
Loose and thick vocal cords produce lower-frequency sound.
Vocal cords in men: about 20 mm long. In women: about 15 mm long. Children: very short.
This is why voices of men, women and children are different.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.6:
sections.aim: To demonstrate how vocal cords produce sound.
sections.materials: Two rubber strips of the same size.
procedure: 1. Take two rubber strips of the same size.
2. Place one piece above the other and stretch them tight.
3. Now blow air through the gap between them (Fig. 10.9a).

items.question: What is the voice box? Where is it located?
items.answer:
The voice box is called the LARYNX.
It is located at the upper end of the windpipe in humans.
It is the organ responsible for producing sound (voice) in human beings.

items.question: How do muscles affect the voice of a person?
items.answer:
Muscles attached to the vocal cords can make the cords tight or loose.
When vocal cords are tight and thin, a higher-pitched (shriller) sound is produced.
When vocal cords are loose and thick, a lower-pitched sound is produced.
This is how the quality of voice changes.

items.question: How does the human voice box produce sound?
items.answer:
The voice box (larynx) is at the upper end of the windpipe.
Two vocal cords are stretched across the larynx, leaving a narrow slit between them.
When the lungs force air through this slit, the vocal cords begin to vibrate.
These vibrations produce sound.
Muscles can change the tightness of the vocal cords, changing the quality of the voice.

items.question: Why are the voices of men, women and children different?
items.answer:
The voices are different because of the different lengths of vocal cords.
Vocal cords in men are about 20 mm long.
In women, they are about 15 mm long.
Children have very short vocal cords.
Shorter and thinner vocal cords vibrate at higher frequency, producing a shriller (higher-pitched) voice.
Longer vocal cords vibrate at lower frequency, producing a deeper voice.
This is why the voices of men, women and children are different.

items.question: Describe an activity to demonstrate how the larynx produces sound in human beings.
items.answer:
ACTIVITY: Take two rubber strips of the same size. Place one above the other and stretch them tight. Now blow air through the gap between them. A sound is heard as the rubber strips vibrate.
Alternatively, take a piece of paper with a narrow slit. Hold it between your fingers and blow air through the slit. A sound is produced.
HOW IT RELATES TO HUMAN VOICE:
In both cases, air forced through a narrow gap causes the material to vibrate and produce sound.
In our throat, the vocal cords act like the rubber strips or the paper slit. The slit between the vocal cords allows air from the lungs to pass. This forces the cords to vibrate and produce sound.

items.question: Explain the role of vocal cords in sound production. How can the pitch of sound be changed?
items.answer:
ROLE OF VOCAL CORDS:
The vocal cords are two stretched membranes inside the larynx (voice box).
They are stretched across the larynx leaving a narrow slit between them.
When lungs force air through this slit, the vocal cords vibrate and produce sound.
CHANGING PITCH:
Muscles attached to the vocal cords can change their tightness:
When muscles make the cords tight and thin: the cords vibrate at higher frequency, producing higher pitch (shriller sound).
When muscles make the cords loose and thick: the cords vibrate at lower frequency, producing lower pitch (deeper sound).
This is how singers and speakers control the pitch of their voice.

items.question: Write a detailed note on the production of sound in human beings. Include the structure involved, the mechanism of sound production, and factors that affect the quality of voice.
items.answer:
ORGANS INVOLVED:
The sound-producing organ in humans is the LARYNX (voice box), located at the upper end of the windpipe.
A hard bump that moves when you swallow is the larynx (Adam's apple), visible on the throat.
STRUCTURE:
Two VOCAL CORDS are stretched across the larynx.
They are arranged in such a way that a narrow slit is left between them for air to pass.
MECHANISM OF SOUND PRODUCTION:
Step 1: The lungs force air upward through the windpipe.
Step 2: Air passes through the narrow slit between the vocal cords.
Step 3: This forces the vocal cords to vibrate.
Step 4: The vibrating vocal cords produce sound.
This is how we speak, sing or make any vocal sound.
FACTORS AFFECTING VOICE QUALITY:
1. TIGHTNESS OF VOCAL CORDS: Muscles can make vocal cords tight (thin) or loose (thick). Tight and thin cords → higher frequency → higher pitch (shriller). Loose and thick cords → lower frequency → lower pitch (deeper).
2. LENGTH OF VOCAL CORDS: Men: ~20 mm long → lower pitch. Women: ~15 mm long → higher pitch. Children: very short → highest pitch. This explains why men, women and children have different sounding voices.
3. PRESSURE OF AIR: More forceful breathing produces louder sound.
CONCLUSION: Sound production in humans is a beautiful combination of the vibration of vocal cords, controlled by air pressure from lungs and muscle tension, producing a wide variety of sounds used for communication.

topics.topic_name: SOUND NEEDS A MEDIUM FOR PROPAGATION

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: MEDIUM: The substance through which sound travels is called the medium. Sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases. Sound CANNOT travel through vacuum (absence of matter).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Sound needs a medium to travel (propagate).
Sound can travel through gases (like air), liquids (like water) and solids (like metal, wood).
Sound CANNOT travel through vacuum. When all air is removed from a vessel (vacuum), no sound can travel through it.
VACUUM: A space where all matter (air) has been removed is called vacuum. Sound cannot travel through vacuum.
Whales and dolphins communicate through sounds in water.
Ultrasound equipment works at frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz and is used in medical investigations.
DIAGRAMS:
Fig. 10.10: Sound needs a medium to travel (cell phone in tumbler with mouth over it)
Fig. 10.11: Sound travelling through water (bell in bucket of water)
Fig. 10.12: Sound travelling through a metre scale
Fig. 10.13: Sound can travel through solids (ear on wooden table)
Fig. 10.14: A toy telephone (sound through strings)

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.7 (Sound through gas - vacuum demonstration):
sections.aim: To show that sound cannot travel through vacuum.
sections.materials: Metal or glass tumbler, cell phone.
procedure: 1. Take a dry metal or glass tumbler. Place a cell phone inside it.
2. Ask a friend to give a ring on this cell phone from another phone.
3. Listen to the ring carefully.
4. Now surround the rim of the tumbler with your hands and put your mouth on the opening. Suck air from the tumbler.
5. Ask your friend to ring again. Listen carefully. Does the sound become fainter as you suck air?
6. Remove the tumbler from your mouth. Does the sound become loud again?
sections.observation: As air is sucked from the tumbler, the sound becomes fainter. When the tumbler is removed and air re-enters, sound becomes loud again.
sections.conclusion: Sound requires a medium (air) to travel. When air is removed, sound becomes fainter, showing that sound cannot travel without a medium.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.8 (Sound through liquids):
sections.aim: To show that sound can travel through liquids.
sections.materials: Bucket or bathtub, clean water, small bell.
procedure: 1. Fill a bucket or bathtub with clean water.
2. Take a small bell in one hand. Shake the bell inside the water to produce sound.
3. Make sure the bell does not touch the body of the bucket or tub.
4. Place your ear gently on the water surface (be careful - water should not enter the ear).
sections.observation: The sound of the bell can be heard even when the ear is placed on the water surface.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.9 (Sound through solids):
sections.aim: To show that sound can travel through solids.
sections.materials: Metre scale or long metal rod.
procedure: 1. Take a metre scale or long metal rod. Hold one end to your ear.
2. Ask a friend to gently scratch or tap at the other end of the scale.
sections.observation: The sound of scratching is clearly heard through the scale (solid).

items.question: What is a medium? Can sound travel through vacuum?
items.answer:
A medium is the substance through which sound travels.
Sound needs a medium (solid, liquid or gas) to travel.
Sound CANNOT travel through vacuum.
When all air is removed from a vessel (creating vacuum), sound cannot travel through it.

items.question: Name the three states of matter through which sound can travel. Give one example for each.
items.answer:
Sound can travel through:
GAS: Sound travels through air (example: we hear people speaking in air).
LIQUID: Sound travels through water (example: whales communicate through water).
SOLID: Sound travels through wood (example: placing ear on a table to hear tapping at the far end).

items.question: How would you show that sound can travel through liquids? Describe an activity.
items.answer: ACTIVITY: Fill a bucket with water. Take a small bell and shake it inside the water. Make sure it does not touch the sides of the bucket. Place your ear gently on the water surface (without letting water enter the ear). You can clearly hear the sound of the bell ringing in water. This proves that sound can travel through liquids (water).

items.question: How would you show that sound can travel through solids? Describe an activity.
items.answer:
ACTIVITY: Take a metre scale or a long metal rod. Hold one end to your ear. Ask a friend to gently scratch or tap at the other end. You can clearly hear the scratching sound through the scale/rod.
You can also perform the same activity by placing your ear at one end of a long wooden or metallic table and asking a friend to scratch the other end.
This proves that sound can travel through solids.

items.question: Prove by an activity that sound cannot travel through vacuum.
items.answer:
ACTIVITY: Take a dry metal or glass tumbler. Place a cell phone inside it. Ask a friend to ring this cell phone. Listen to the ring carefully. Now cover the rim of the tumbler with your hands and put your mouth over the opening. Suck air out of the tumbler. Ask your friend to ring again. OBSERVATION: As air is sucked out, the sound of the ring becomes fainter. When the tumbler is removed from your mouth and air re-enters, the ring becomes loud again.
ACTIVITY EXPLANATION: As we suck air out, we create a partial vacuum inside the tumbler. The lesser the amount of air (medium), the fainter the sound. If all air were completely removed, no sound would be heard at all.
CONCLUSION: Sound needs air (a medium) to travel. It cannot travel through vacuum.

items.question: Give three examples to show that sound can travel through solids, liquids and gases.
items.answer:
SOUND THROUGH GASES: We hear each other speak in normal air. When someone knocks at a door, the sound travels through air to reach our ears.
SOUND THROUGH LIQUIDS: Whales and dolphins communicate by producing sounds that travel through ocean water. If you shake a bell inside water and place your ear on the water surface, you can hear the bell ringing.
SOUND THROUGH SOLIDS: If you place your ear at one end of a long metal rod or table and a friend taps the other end gently, you can hear the tapping clearly. Children use toy telephones (two cans connected by a string) where sound travels through the string.
CONCLUSION: Sound can travel through all three states of matter - solid, liquid and gas - but it cannot travel through vacuum.

items.question: Describe the three activities to demonstrate that sound can travel through solid, liquid and gas, and also show that sound cannot travel through vacuum.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 1 - SOUND THROUGH SOLIDS:

sections.label: ACTIVITY 2 - SOUND THROUGH LIQUIDS:
sections.observation: The ring of the bell is clearly heard.

sections.label: ACTIVITY 3 - SOUND THROUGH GAS AND VACUUM:
sections.observation: Sound becomes fainter as air is removed. When air re-enters, sound becomes loud again.
sections.conclusion:
Sound travels through gases. When air is removed (vacuum), sound cannot travel. This proves sound cannot travel through vacuum.
OVERALL CONCLUSION: Sound needs a medium to travel. It can pass through solids, liquids and gases, but not through vacuum. This is why there is complete silence in outer space (which is a vacuum).

items.question: Sound CANNOT travel through
items.explanation: Sound needs a medium (matter) to travel. Vacuum has no matter, so sound cannot propagate through it.

items.question: Which of the following is a medium for sound?
items.explanation: Sound can travel through water (liquid), air (gas) and solids. It cannot travel through vacuum or outer space.

items.question: In Activity 10.8, the sound of a bell shaken in water was heard by placing the ear on the water surface. This proves:

items.question: In Activity 10.7, as air was sucked out of the tumbler containing the ringing cell phone, what happened to the sound?
items.explanation: As air was removed, the medium for sound decreased. With less medium, the sound became fainter. This shows sound requires a medium (air) to travel.

items.question: Which animals use sound to communicate under water?
items.explanation: Whales and dolphins communicate with each other by producing sounds that travel through ocean water, showing that sound can travel through liquids.

items.question: A boy places his ear on one end of a metal rail and another person taps the other end. The sound travels to the boy through:
items.explanation: Sound can travel through both the solid metal rail and through the air around it. Both paths are available, though sound travels faster through the solid.

items.question: What does the term vacuum mean?

options.C: A space from which all matter (air) has been removed
options.D: A space filled with solid material

items.explanation: Vacuum is a space in which all air (and other matter) has been removed. Since sound needs a medium to travel, it cannot travel through vacuum.

items.question: Why is there complete silence in outer space even though explosions of stars occur?

options.A: The explosions are too small to produce sound

options.C: Human ears are not sensitive enough
options.D: Sound travels too slowly to reach Earth

items.explanation: Outer space is essentially vacuum - it has no medium for sound to travel through. Therefore, even massive stellar explosions produce no sound that can travel through space.

items.question: In Activity 10.7, if all air could be completely removed from the tumbler, what would happen?

options.A: The sound would become very loud
options.B: No sound would be heard at all

items.explanation: Complete removal of air creates a perfect vacuum. Since sound needs a medium to travel, complete vacuum means no medium and therefore no sound would be heard. This is the concept of sound not travelling through vacuum.

topics.topic_name: WE HEAR SOUND THROUGH OUR EARS

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The EAR is the organ of hearing. The EARDRUM (tympanic membrane) is the thin stretched membrane inside the ear that vibrates in response to sound waves and sends signals to the brain.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The outer part of the ear is funnel-shaped to collect sound.
Sound travels down a canal (ear canal) to the eardrum.
The eardrum is a thin stretched membrane at the end of the ear canal.
Sound vibrations cause the eardrum to vibrate.
The eardrum sends vibrations to the inner ear, which sends signals to the brain.
This process is called HEARING.
IMPORTANT: Never put a sharp, pointed or hard object into the ear - it can damage the eardrum. Damaged eardrum can impair hearing.

HEARING IMPAIRMENT: Total hearing impairment (from birth) is rare. Partial disability is generally caused by disease, injury or age. Children with impaired hearing need special care and can learn sign language to communicate.
DIAGRAMS:
Fig. 10.15: Understanding the action of an eardrum (tin-can model)
Fig. 10.16: Human ear (showing eardrum and inner ear)

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.10 (Model of eardrum):
sections.aim: To understand how the eardrum functions.
sections.materials: Plastic or tin-can, rubber balloon, rubber band, dry cereal grains.
procedure: 1. Take a plastic or tin-can. Cut its ends.
2. Stretch a piece of rubber balloon across one end of the can and fasten it with a rubber band.
3. Put four or five grains of dry cereal on the stretched rubber.
4. Ask your friend to speak "Hurrey, Hurrey" from the open end of the can.
sections.observation: The grains on the rubber jump up and down when your friend speaks.
sections.conclusion: Sound vibrations travel through the air in the can and cause the rubber membrane (like the eardrum) to vibrate. This is exactly how our eardrum works - it vibrates when sound waves reach it.

items.question: What is the eardrum? Where is it located?
items.answer:
The eardrum is a thin stretched membrane located at the end of the ear canal.
It is inside the ear, just beyond the ear canal.
When sound waves reach the eardrum, it vibrates and sends the vibrations to the inner ear and then to the brain.

items.question: Why should we never put sharp objects into our ears?
items.answer:
The eardrum is a delicate, thin stretched membrane inside the ear.
Putting sharp, pointed or hard objects into the ear can damage the eardrum.
A damaged eardrum can cause impairment of hearing - partial or permanent.
Therefore, we must never put anything sharp into our ears.

items.question: Describe the structure of the outer ear and explain how it helps in hearing.
items.answer:
The outer ear is shaped like a funnel.
This funnel shape helps to collect sound from the surroundings.
Sound collected by the outer ear travels down a canal called the ear canal.
At the end of the ear canal is the eardrum (thin stretched membrane).
Sound vibrations strike the eardrum and cause it to vibrate.
The eardrum sends vibrations to the inner ear, which sends signals to the brain, completing the process of hearing.

items.question: Describe Activity 10.10 (tin-can model). What does this activity demonstrate?
items.answer:
ACTIVITY: Take a tin or plastic can. Cut its ends. Stretch a piece of rubber balloon across one end and fasten it with a rubber band. Put 4-5 dry cereal grains on the stretched rubber. Ask a friend to speak "Hurrey, Hurrey" from the open end of the can.
OBSERVATION: The cereal grains jump up and down when the friend speaks.
CONCLUSION: Sound vibrations from the friend's voice travel through the air in the can and cause the rubber membrane to vibrate. The vibrating membrane makes the grains jump. This demonstrates how our eardrum functions: it is a stretched membrane that vibrates in response to sound vibrations reaching it.

items.question: Explain the process of hearing in humans from sound source to brain.
items.answer:
Step 1 - COLLECTION: The funnel-shaped outer ear collects sound waves from the surroundings.
Step 2 - TRAVEL: The sound waves travel down the ear canal.
Step 3 - EARDRUM VIBRATION: At the end of the ear canal, sound waves strike the eardrum (thin stretched membrane). The eardrum vibrates.
Step 4 - TRANSMISSION: The vibrating eardrum sends the vibrations to the inner ear.
Step 5 - SIGNAL TO BRAIN: From the inner ear, the signal goes to the brain.
Step 6 - HEARING: The brain interprets the signal as sound - this is the sense of hearing.
Thus, hearing is the process by which sound energy is converted to nerve signals that the brain can interpret.

items.question: What is hearing impairment? How can children with impaired hearing be helped?
items.answer:
HEARING IMPAIRMENT: Reduced or absent ability to hear sounds is called hearing impairment.
CAUSES: Total hearing impairment from birth is rare. Partial disability is generally caused by disease, injury or age.
EFFECTS ON CHILDREN: Since speech develops as a direct result of hearing, a child with hearing loss may also have defective speech.
HOW TO HELP:
Children with impaired hearing need special care.
By learning sign language, they can communicate effectively.
Technological devices (hearing aids) for hearing-impaired people have made it possible for them to improve their quality of life.
Society can do much to improve the living environment for hearing-impaired children and help them lead normal lives.

items.question: Explain the anatomy and functioning of the human ear in detail. Why is the eardrum said to be like a stretched rubber sheet? Include the safety message.
items.answer:
ANATOMY OF THE HUMAN EAR:
The human ear has three main parts - outer ear, middle ear and inner ear.
OUTER EAR: The visible funnel-shaped outer ear collects sound from the surroundings. Its funnel shape is specially designed to gather sound waves from the environment.
EAR CANAL: Sound travels from the outer ear down a narrow canal (the ear canal).
EARDRUM (TYMPANIC MEMBRANE): At the end of the ear canal is a thin, tightly stretched membrane called the eardrum. It is like a stretched rubber sheet - thin, elastic and sensitive to vibrations.
INNER EAR: Beyond the eardrum is the inner ear, which contains delicate structures for detecting vibrations.
FUNCTIONING:
1. Sound waves enter the funnel-shaped outer ear.
2. They travel down the ear canal.
3. They strike the eardrum, causing it to vibrate.
4. The eardrum (like a stretched rubber sheet) vibrates to and fro in response to sound waves.
5. These vibrations are transmitted to the inner ear.
6. The inner ear sends nerve signals to the brain.
7. The brain interprets these signals as sound - this is hearing.
WHY EARDRUM IS LIKE A STRETCHED RUBBER SHEET:
The eardrum is very thin and stretched tight, just like a piece of stretched rubber. When sound waves (pressure variations) reach it, the eardrum vibrates back and forth, exactly like a rubber membrane being pushed and released repeatedly. This vibration carries the pattern of the sound to the inner ear.
SAFETY MESSAGE:
The eardrum is extremely delicate. We must NEVER put sharp, pointed or hard objects into our ear. Such objects can pierce or damage the eardrum. A damaged eardrum can cause partial or permanent hearing loss. This is why doctors and teachers strongly advise against putting anything into the ear.

items.explanation: The stretched rubber balloon across the tin-can models the eardrum (tympanic membrane), which is also a thin, tightly stretched membrane that vibrates in response to sound.

items.question: What happens if the eardrum of a person is permanently damaged?

options.A: The person can hear better because the inner ear is exposed
options.B: The person suffers hearing impairment (partial or permanent deafness)
options.C: The person can still hear normally

items.explanation: The eardrum is essential for converting sound waves into mechanical vibrations that reach the inner ear. If permanently damaged, the person will suffer hearing impairment, which can be partial or permanent.

topics.topic_name: AMPLITUDE, TIME PERIOD AND FREQUENCY OF A VIBRATION

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
AMPLITUDE: The maximum displacement of a vibrating object from its rest (equilibrium) position is called amplitude. It is a measure of how far the object moves from its rest position.
TIME PERIOD: The time taken by a vibrating object to complete one full oscillation (one complete to and fro motion) is called the time period. Symbol: T.
FREQUENCY: The number of oscillations (complete to and fro motions) made by a vibrating body in one second is called frequency. Symbol: f or n.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Vibration = oscillatory motion = to and fro motion.
LOUDNESS depends on amplitude. Larger amplitude → louder sound. Loudness is proportional to the square of amplitude. If amplitude doubles, loudness increases 4 times.
Loudness is expressed in decibels (dB).
PITCH depends on frequency. Higher frequency → higher pitch (shriller sound). Lower frequency → lower pitch (deeper sound).
Frequency is expressed in HERTZ (Hz). Symbol: Hz.
1 Hz = 1 oscillation per second.
Time period and frequency are related: Frequency = 1 / Time period. (f = 1/T)
A drum has low frequency → low-pitched (deep) sound.
A whistle has high frequency → high-pitched (shrill) sound.
A bird makes a high-pitched sound; a lion makes a low-pitched roar.

sections.label: FORMULA:
items: Number of oscillations = frequency x time
Note: Above 80 dB, noise becomes physically painful.
- Fig. 10.17: Thermocol ball touching the vibrating glass tumbler (demonstrating amplitude)
- Fig. 10.18: Frequency determines the pitch of a sound (drum = low frequency/low pitch, whistle = high frequency/high pitch)

sections.label: ACTIVITY 10.11 (Amplitude and Loudness):
sections.aim: To understand amplitude and its relation to loudness.
sections.materials: Metallic tumbler, tablespoon, small thermocol ball.
procedure: 1. Take a metallic tumbler and a tablespoon.
2. Strike the tablespoon gently at the brim of the tumbler. Listen to the sound.
3. Now bang the spoon harder on the tumbler. Hear the sound. Is the sound louder?
4. Suspend a small thermocol ball touching the rim of the tumbler.
5. Vibrate the tumbler by striking gently. See how far the ball is displaced.
6. Strike harder. The ball is displaced further.
sections.observation: Harder striking produces louder sound and greater displacement of the ball (larger amplitude).
sections.conclusion:
Loudness is related to amplitude. Larger amplitude → louder sound.

EXAMPLE PROBLEMS:
EXAMPLE 1: A pendulum oscillates 40 times in 4 seconds. Find its time period and frequency.
Number of oscillations = 40, Time = 4 seconds
Time period T = Total time / Number of oscillations = 4/40 = 0.1 second
Frequency f = 1/T = 1/0.1 = 10 Hz
OR: Frequency = Number of oscillations / Time = 40/4 = 10 Hz

EXAMPLE 2: A mosquito vibrates its wings 500 times per second. What is the time period?
Frequency f = 500 Hz
Time period T = 1/f = 1/500 = 0.002 seconds

items.question: What is amplitude? How does it affect loudness?
items.answer:
AMPLITUDE: The maximum displacement of a vibrating object from its rest position is called amplitude.
EFFECT ON LOUDNESS: Loudness of sound is proportional to the square of the amplitude. Larger amplitude of vibration produces louder sound. Smaller amplitude produces faint sound.

items.question: What is frequency? What is its unit?
items.answer:
FREQUENCY: The number of oscillations (complete to and fro motions) made by a vibrating body in one second is called frequency.
UNIT: Frequency is expressed in HERTZ (Hz). Symbol: Hz.
1 Hz means 1 oscillation per second.

items.question: A pendulum oscillates 40 times in 4 seconds. Find its time period and frequency.
items.answer:
Given: Number of oscillations = 40, Total time = 4 seconds
TIME PERIOD: T = Total time / Number of oscillations = 4/40 = 0.1 second
FREQUENCY: f = Number of oscillations / Time = 40/4 = 10 Hz
OR: f = 1/T = 1/0.1 = 10 Hz
Therefore, time period = 0.1 s and frequency = 10 Hz.

items.question: What is pitch? How is pitch related to frequency?
items.answer:
PITCH: The shrillness or quality of a sound that depends on its frequency is called pitch.
RELATION WITH FREQUENCY: The frequency determines the pitch of a sound.
Higher the frequency of vibration → higher the pitch → shriller the sound.
Lower the frequency of vibration → lower the pitch → deeper the sound.
EXAMPLES: A drum vibrates at low frequency → produces low-pitched deep sound. A whistle vibrates at high frequency → produces high-pitched shrill sound. Birds make high-pitched sounds; lions make low-pitched roars.

items.question: Write the relationship between time period and frequency. A mosquito vibrates its wings 500 times per second. Find its time period.
items.answer:
RELATIONSHIP: Frequency and time period are reciprocals of each other.
f = 1/T and T = 1/f
Where f = frequency (in Hz) and T = time period (in seconds).
CALCULATION:
Given: The mosquito's wings vibrate 500 times per second.
Therefore, frequency f = 500 Hz
Time period T = 1/f = 1/500 = 0.002 seconds
The time period of the mosquito's wing vibration is 0.002 seconds.

items.question: Explain how the loudness of sound is related to amplitude. Describe the activity to demonstrate this.
items.answer:
RELATION: Loudness of sound is proportional to the square of the amplitude of vibration.
If amplitude doubles → loudness increases 4 times.
If amplitude is small → sound is faint (quiet).
If amplitude is large → sound is loud.
Loudness is expressed in decibels (dB).
ACTIVITY: Take a metallic tumbler and tablespoon. Strike the tablespoon gently on the rim of the tumbler - a soft sound is heard. Bang harder - a louder sound is heard. Suspend a thermocol ball touching the rim. When struck gently, the ball moves a small distance (small amplitude). When struck harder, the ball moves farther (large amplitude). The louder sound corresponds to larger amplitude.
CONCLUSION: Loudness increases with amplitude. Specifically, loudness is proportional to the square of amplitude.

items.question: Define amplitude, time period and frequency of a vibration. Write the formula relating time period and frequency. Solve: (a) A pendulum oscillates 40 times in 4 seconds - find time period and frequency. (b) A mosquito vibrates wings at 500 Hz - find time period.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
AUDIBLE SOUNDS: Sounds that can be detected by the human ear are called audible sounds.
INAUDIBLE SOUNDS: Sounds that cannot be detected by the human ear are called inaudible sounds.
INFRASOUND: Sounds with frequency LESS THAN 20 Hz (inaudible to humans).
ULTRASOUND: Sounds with frequency MORE THAN 20,000 Hz (inaudible to humans).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: The human ear can hear sounds in the frequency range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Sounds with frequency less than 20 Hz or greater than 20,000 Hz are inaudible to humans.
The audible frequency range is roughly 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
Some animals can hear frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz. Example: DOGS. Police use high-frequency dog whistles that dogs can hear but humans cannot.
ULTRASOUND equipment works at frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz. It is used in medicine to investigate and track many medical problems.
Higher the frequency → higher the pitch → shriller the sound.

items.question: What is the audible range of sound for human beings?
items.answer:
The range of audible frequencies for human beings is roughly from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
Sounds with frequency below 20 Hz (infrasound) and above 20,000 Hz (ultrasound) are inaudible to humans.

items.question: What is ultrasound? Give one use.
items.answer:
Ultrasound refers to sounds with frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz (20 kHz).
These sounds are beyond the upper limit of human hearing and are inaudible to us.
USE: Ultrasound equipment is used in medicine to investigate and track many medical problems (like ultrasound scanning of internal organs).

items.question: Why do dogs respond to dog whistles that humans cannot hear?
items.answer:
Dog whistles produce sounds at frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz.
The human ear can hear only sounds in the range 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Sounds above 20,000 Hz are inaudible to humans.
However, dogs can hear sounds of frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz.
Therefore, when a police officer blows a dog whistle, the dog can hear the high-frequency sound and responds, while the officer cannot hear it.

items.question: Why can we not hear the vibrations produced by a pendulum of very low frequency?
items.answer:
A pendulum of very low frequency (for example, one oscillation per second = 1 Hz) produces sound waves of 1 Hz.
The human ear can detect sounds only in the frequency range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Sounds of frequency less than 20 Hz (infrasound) are below the threshold of human hearing.
Therefore, we cannot hear the vibrations of a very slow pendulum.
However, some animals can hear such low-frequency sounds.

items.question: Distinguish between audible and inaudible sounds. Give examples.
items.answer:
AUDIBLE SOUNDS:
Definition: Sounds that can be detected by the human ear.
Frequency range: 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Examples: Human speech (300-3000 Hz), musical instruments, sound of traffic, thunder.

INAUDIBLE SOUNDS:
Definition: Sounds that cannot be detected by the human ear.
Types:
(i) Infrasound: Frequency less than 20 Hz. Example: vibrations produced by a very slowly oscillating pendulum.
(ii) Ultrasound: Frequency more than 20,000 Hz. Example: sounds of dog whistles, bat echolocation, ultrasound equipment used in medicine.

KEY DIFFERENCE: Audible sounds are within human hearing range (20 Hz - 20,000 Hz). Inaudible sounds are outside this range - either too low (infrasound) or too high (ultrasound) in frequency.

items.question: What is the role of ultrasound in medicine? Why is it possible to use ultrasound but not very low-frequency sounds for this purpose?
items.answer:
ULTRASOUND IN MEDICINE:
Ultrasound equipment works at frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz.
It is used for investigating and tracking many medical problems:
- Ultrasound scans (sonography) are used to view internal organs like the kidney, liver, uterus.
- It is used to monitor the growth of a baby during pregnancy.
- It helps detect tumours, gallstones, kidney stones and other abnormalities.
WHY ULTRASOUND IS SUITABLE:
Ultrasound waves have very short wavelengths (due to high frequency), which allows them to create detailed images of internal organs.
They are above the human hearing range (20,000 Hz), so the patient does not experience any discomfort from the sound.
Very low-frequency sounds (infrasound) would have very long wavelengths and cannot create detailed images of small internal structures.

items.question: Explain the concept of audible and inaudible sounds with examples. What is the role of frequency in determining whether a sound is audible or not? Discuss animals that can hear sounds inaudible to humans.
items.answer:
AUDIBLE SOUNDS:
Sounds that can be detected by the human ear are called audible sounds.
The human ear responds to sounds in the frequency range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz.
Any sound within this range (20 Hz to 20,000 Hz) is audible to humans.
Examples: Human conversation (300-3000 Hz), musical instruments, vehicle horns, thunder.

INAUDIBLE SOUNDS:
Sounds outside the human audible range are inaudible:
(a) INFRASOUND (below 20 Hz): Very low-frequency sounds. Example: Vibrations of the ground during an earthquake, sound produced by a very slowly swinging pendulum.
(b) ULTRASOUND (above 20,000 Hz): Very high-frequency sounds. Example: Dog whistles, bat echolocation signals, ultrasound medical equipment.

ROLE OF FREQUENCY:
Frequency directly determines whether a sound is audible:
Too low (< 20 Hz) → below the lower threshold → inaudible (infrasound).
In range (20 Hz - 20,000 Hz) → within audible range → audible.
Too high (> 20,000 Hz) → above the upper threshold → inaudible (ultrasound).

ANIMALS WITH DIFFERENT HEARING RANGES:
DOGS: Can hear frequencies higher than 20,000 Hz. Police use high-frequency dog whistles that dogs respond to but humans cannot hear.
BATS: Can hear and produce ultrasound (above 20,000 Hz). They use echolocation to navigate and find prey in darkness.
WHALES AND DOLPHINS: Can produce and detect both very low (infrasound) and high (ultrasound) frequency sounds for communication and navigation in water.
CONCLUSION: The hearing range differs from species to species. Humans can hear 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Bats and dogs can hear much higher frequencies. Some animals like elephants can detect infrasound (below 20 Hz).

items.explanation: Sounds with frequencies above 20,000 Hz (the upper limit of human hearing) are called ultrasound. They are inaudible to humans.

items.explanation: Sounds below 20 Hz (lower limit of human hearing) are called infrasound. They are inaudible to the human ear.

options.B: It helps detect internal organ abnormalities without surgery
options.C: It is louder than normal sound

items.explanation: Ultrasound at high frequencies can create detailed images of internal organs (liver, kidney, uterus, etc.) and detect abnormalities like tumours and kidney stones, without any invasive procedure.

items.question: A bat can navigate in darkness using echolocation. This works because bats can

options.A: See in darkness using special eyes

items.explanation: Bats produce ultrasound waves and detect their echoes reflected from obstacles. This echolocation system allows them to navigate and hunt in complete darkness.

items.question: Which of the following sounds has the highest pitch?
items.explanation: Pitch is directly related to frequency. The higher the frequency, the higher the pitch. Among the options, 20,000 Hz has the highest frequency, so it has the highest pitch.

items.question: Voice of which of the following is likely to have minimum frequency?
items.explanation: Men have the longest vocal cords (~20 mm), which vibrate at the lowest frequency, producing the deepest (lowest pitched) voice. Therefore, a man's voice has the minimum frequency among humans.

items.question: The ultrasound equipment works at frequencies above 20,000 Hz. If it produces a sound of frequency 40,000 Hz, what is its time period?
items.explanation: T = 1/f = 1/40,000 = 0.000025 seconds (25 microseconds). Very high frequency means very short time period.

items.question: An elephant is said to communicate using infrasound. This means the elephant uses sounds of frequency
items.explanation: Infrasound has frequencies below 20 Hz. Elephants can produce and detect infrasound waves, which can travel long distances. Humans cannot hear these as they are below the lower threshold of human hearing (20 Hz).

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text:
NOISE: An unpleasant, irritating or unwanted sound is called noise.
MUSICAL SOUND: A sound that is pleasing to the ear is called musical sound (music).

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: Not all sounds are pleasing. Some are pleasant and some cause discomfort.
Sounds from musical instruments (harmonium, sitar, etc.) are musical sounds.
Sounds from construction sites, vehicle horns, loudspeakers etc. are noise.
If all students in a classroom speak together, the combined sound becomes noise.
Even a musical sound can become noise if it is too loud.
The difference between noise and music is largely based on the quality (regularity) of vibration and the sensation it produces on the ear.

items.question: What is the difference between noise and music?
items.answer:
NOISE: An unpleasant, irritating or unwanted sound is called noise. It causes discomfort to the ear.
MUSIC: A pleasant, regular, agreeable sound is called musical sound (music). It pleases the ear.
Example: Sound from a sitar or harmonium is music. Sound from a construction site or honking vehicles is noise.

items.question: Can music become noise? When?
items.answer:
Yes, music can become noise if it becomes too loud.
For example, the sound of a sitar played at a normal volume is music.
But if the same sound is played at an extremely high volume, it becomes irritating and discomforting - that is, it becomes noise.
Therefore, even a musical sound becomes noise if the loudness exceeds a comfortable level.

items.question: Give examples of noise and music from everyday life.
items.answer:
EXAMPLES OF NOISE:
1. Sound from construction work going on in the neighbourhood.
2. Sound of vehicle horns on a busy road.
3. All students in a class speaking together.
4. Sound of crackers exploding.

EXAMPLES OF MUSICAL SOUNDS:
1. Sound of a harmonium or sitar being played.
2. A person singing a song.
3. Sound of a flute or violin being played.
4. Pleasant sounds from wind chimes.

items.question: Why is the sound produced when all students in a classroom speak together called noise and not music?
items.answer:
When all students in a classroom speak together, each student produces a different sound at a different frequency, amplitude and timing.
These many irregular, unrelated vibrations combine to produce a confused, disorganised sound.
This kind of irregular, unpleasant, disorganised sound is called noise.
In contrast, music has regular, organised vibrations that are pleasing to the ear.
Since the combined sound of all students speaking together is unpleasant and disorganised, it is noise and not music.

items.question: What distinguishes a musical sound from noise? Is it possible for a musical instrument to produce noise?
items.answer:
MUSICAL SOUND VS NOISE:
Musical sound has regular, organised vibrations that produce a pleasant sensation on the ear.
Noise has irregular, disorganised vibrations that produce an unpleasant sensation.
FEATURES OF MUSICAL SOUND:
- Regular and periodic vibrations.
- Pleasing to the ear.
- Produced by musical instruments or trained voices.
CAN MUSICAL INSTRUMENTS PRODUCE NOISE?
Yes, a musical instrument can produce noise. Example: The string of a sitar gives out a musical sound. But if a musical sound becomes too loud, would it remain melodious? No - it would become noise. A sitar played at very high volume in a small room can produce an uncomfortable, unpleasant sound, which is noise. Therefore, loudness is also an important factor in distinguishing music from noise.

items.question: You are enjoying music from a speaker but your neighbour complains about noise. Explain this situation with reference to the definitions of noise and music.
items.answer:
This situation illustrates that noise and music are subjective to some extent.
YOUR PERSPECTIVE: You are listening to music from a speaker at a volume that is pleasant for you. The regular, pleasing vibrations of the music are within your comfortable range, so you perceive it as music.
NEIGHBOUR'S PERSPECTIVE: The same sound at the same volume may be too loud or unwanted for your neighbour who is not interested in it. Any excessive or unwanted sound in the environment is noise. Since the neighbour does not want the sound and finds it disturbing, it is noise for them.
SCIENTIFIC EXPLANATION: Noise is defined as an unpleasant or unwanted sound. Even musical sound can become noise if it is too loud (above comfortable dB levels) or unwanted by the listener. This is why noise pollution includes loud music - because a sound that is pleasant for one person can be noise for another.
CONCLUSION: Whether a sound is music or noise depends on the type of vibration (regular vs irregular) and the loudness and context. Even music becomes noise when too loud.

items.question: What is the difference between noise and music? Explain with examples. Also discuss whether music can become noise and give the scientific reasoning.

sections.label: DEFINITION OF NOISE:
sections.text:
Noise is an unpleasant, irregular, irritating or unwanted sound.
It is caused by irregular vibrations.
It causes discomfort to the ear and the listener.
EXAMPLES OF NOISE: Sound of construction work, honking of vehicles, a crowd of people all talking at once, sound of crackers, sounds from machines in a factory.

sections.label: DEFINITION OF MUSICAL SOUND:
sections.text:
Music is a pleasant, regular, organised sound that is agreeable to the ear.
It is caused by regular, periodic vibrations.
It gives a pleasant sensation.
EXAMPLES OF MUSICAL SOUNDS: Sound of a sitar, harmonium, tabla, flute; a person singing a song; sound of wind chimes.

KEY DIFFERENCES:
| Feature          | Noise                  | Music                  |
|------------------|------------------------|------------------------|
| Vibrations       | Irregular              | Regular, periodic      |
| Sensation        | Unpleasant, irritating | Pleasant, agreeable    |
| Source examples  | Traffic, machines      | Instruments, singing   |
| Effect           | Causes discomfort      | Pleases the ear        |

CAN MUSIC BECOME NOISE?
Yes, music can become noise. Two conditions make this happen:
(a) EXCESSIVE LOUDNESS: If the volume of music becomes too loud (above 80 dB), it causes physical discomfort. Even pleasant music at very high volume becomes noise.
(b) UNWANTED SOUND: If a person is not interested in the music or is disturbed by it, it becomes noise for that person.
SCIENTIFIC REASONING: The boundary between music and noise is not absolute. It depends on loudness (amplitude), frequency, and the context (is it wanted or not?). This is why noise pollution laws include restrictions on loud music in residential areas.
CONCLUSION: Music and noise differ mainly in the nature of vibrations (regular vs irregular) and the comfort level of the listener. But even music can cross the line to become noise when it is too loud or unwanted.

options.B: Any sound that is unwanted in a given context can be noise
options.C: Libraries are made of noise-absorbing material

items.explanation: Noise is not only about irregular vibrations - it is also about unwanted sound. In a library, silence is required for study. Even a whisper, which is a soft sound, becomes noise because it is unwanted in that context.

items.question: A person says "I cannot study because of the loud music next door." The loud music is considered noise by this person because

options.B: The sound is from a stringed instrument
options.C: The sound is excessive and unwanted, disturbing concentration
options.D: The frequency of music is below 20 Hz

items.explanation: The music is too loud (excessive amplitude) and is unwanted by the student. By definition, any excessive or unwanted sound is noise. This is the basis of noise pollution - even music at high volumes becomes noise pollution.

sections.label: DEFINITION:
sections.text: The presence of excessive or unwanted sounds in the environment is called NOISE POLLUTION.

sections.label: KEY POINTS:
points: CAUSES OF NOISE POLLUTION: Sound of vehicles, explosions (crackers), machines, loudspeakers, television and radio at high volumes, kitchen appliances (desert coolers, air conditioners).
HARMS OF NOISE POLLUTION:
1. Lack of sleep (insomnia)
2. Hypertension (high blood pressure)
3. Anxiety
4. Many other health disorders
5. Temporary or permanent hearing impairment
Note: A person exposed to loud sounds continuously may get temporary or even permanent impairment of hearing.
MEASURES TO CONTROL NOISE POLLUTION:
1. Silencing devices in aircraft engines, transport vehicles, industrial machines and home appliances.
2. All noisy operations must be conducted away from residential areas.
3. Noise-producing industries should be located away from residential areas.
4. Use of automobile horns should be minimised.
5. TV and music systems should be run at low volumes.
6. Trees must be planted along roads and around buildings to cut down noise.
HEARING IMPAIRMENT (special box in textbook):
Total hearing impairment from birth is rare and is usually the result of birth itself.
Partial disability is generally caused by disease, injury or age.
Children with hearing impairment need special care.
By learning sign language, such children can communicate.
Speech develops as the direct result of hearing; so a child with hearing loss may have defective speech.
Technological devices for the hearing-impaired have made it possible to improve quality of life.
Society can do much to improve living environment for the hearing-impaired.

sections.label: ADDITIONAL FACTS (DO YOU KNOW?):
sections.text: Golconda fort, near Hyderabad, is one of the most magnificent forts in India. It is famous for its many engineering and architectural marvels. One remarkable feature is a dome near the entrance. A hand-clap at a particular point under the dome reverberates and can be heard at the highest point of the fort - about a kilometre away. This was designed as a warning system. If a guard saw a suspicious movement outside the fort, he clapped at that point under the dome, and the army inside the fort was alerted to the approaching danger.

items.question: What is noise pollution?
items.answer:
The presence of excessive or unwanted sounds in the environment is called noise pollution.
It is similar to air pollution, but instead of unwanted gases or particles, it involves unwanted sounds.
It is caused by vehicles, machines, loudspeakers, crackers, industry and household appliances.

items.question: List any four causes of noise pollution.
items.answer:
Four causes of noise pollution:
1. Sound of vehicles (buses, trucks, motorcycles) honking horns.
2. Explosions such as bursting of crackers.
3. Loudspeakers used at high volumes.
4. Television and radio at high volumes.
(Other causes: machines in factories, kitchen appliances like desert coolers and air conditioners.)

items.question: What are the harmful effects of noise pollution on human health?
items.answer:
Effects of noise pollution on human health:
1. LACK OF SLEEP: Excessive noise prevents proper sleep (insomnia).
2. HYPERTENSION: Noise causes high blood pressure (hypertension).
3. ANXIETY: Constant exposure to noise causes anxiety and stress.
4. HEALTH DISORDERS: Many other health disorders can be caused by excessive noise.
5. HEARING IMPAIRMENT: A person continuously exposed to loud sounds may suffer temporary or even permanent impairment of hearing.

items.question: List any four measures to control noise pollution.
items.answer:
Four measures to control noise pollution:
1. SILENCING DEVICES: Silencing devices must be installed in aircraft engines, transport vehicles, industrial machines and home appliances.
2. INDUSTRY LOCATION: All noisy operations and noise-producing industries must be set up away from residential areas.
3. REDUCED HORN USE: Use of automobile horns should be minimised.
4. TREE PLANTATION: Trees must be planted along roads and around buildings. Trees absorb sound and help reduce noise pollution.

items.question: Your family has been offered two houses - one on the roadside and another three lanes away. Which house would you suggest they buy? Explain your answer based on noise pollution.
items.answer:
I would suggest my family buy the house THREE LANES AWAY FROM THE ROADSIDE.
REASON - NOISE POLLUTION:
Roadside houses are exposed to constant noise from:
- Sound of vehicle horns (buses, trucks, motorcycles) - which is around 70-80 dB.
- Constant traffic noise which can be disturbing.
- Sound of brakes, engines and horns throughout the day and night.
HARMFUL EFFECTS:
This constant exposure to noise can cause lack of sleep, hypertension, anxiety and health disorders.
Long-term exposure may lead to hearing impairment.
ADVANTAGES OF LANE HOUSE:
Three lanes away from the road, the noise level is much lower.
There is more greenery (trees may be present) which further reduces noise.
Better sleep, less stress and better overall health.
CONCLUSION: Living near a noisy road exposes the family to noise pollution. The house away from the road would be healthier and more comfortable. This is why we must consider noise pollution when choosing a place to live.

items.question: How can trees help in reducing noise pollution? Describe other measures too.
items.answer:
TREES AS NOISE BARRIERS:
Trees act as natural sound barriers. When planted along roads and around buildings, they absorb sound waves and prevent them from spreading further. Leaves and branches of trees scatter and absorb sound energy, reducing the level of noise reaching homes. Dense plantations of trees (green belts) around noisy areas can significantly cut down noise pollution.
OTHER MEASURES:
1. SILENCING DEVICES: Fitting silencers in vehicles, aircraft engines, industrial machines and home appliances (like air conditioners) reduces the noise they produce.
2. INDUSTRY CONTROL: Noise-producing industries and operations must be located far from residential areas.
3. HORN RESTRICTIONS: Unnecessary use of automobile horns must be discouraged. "No Horn" zones near hospitals, schools and residential areas.
4. VOLUME CONTROL: Television, music systems and loudspeakers should be run at low volumes, especially in residential areas.
5. NOISE-PROOF ROOMS: In areas where noisy operations are unavoidable, noise-insulating rooms can be constructed.
CONCLUSION: Controlling noise pollution requires a combination of technological solutions (silencers, sound-proofing), urban planning (locating industries away from homes), regulation (horn restrictions, volume limits) and natural solutions (tree planting).

items.question: Write a detailed note on noise pollution covering: definition, causes, harmful effects and measures to control it. Also discuss the role of society in helping hearing-impaired individuals.
items.answer:
NOISE POLLUTION:
DEFINITION: The presence of excessive or unwanted sounds in the environment is called noise pollution. Just as air pollution involves unwanted substances in air, noise pollution involves unwanted sounds in the environment.

CAUSES:
1. Road traffic: Vehicles, automobile horns, engines of buses and trucks.
2. Explosions: Bursting of crackers during festivals.
3. Electronic devices: Television, radio, loudspeakers at high volumes.
4. Household appliances: Desert coolers, air conditioners, kitchen appliances.
5. Industry: Machines, generators and industrial equipment.
6. Construction: Drilling, hammering at construction sites.

HARMFUL EFFECTS ON HEALTH:
Presence of excessive noise causes:
1. Lack of sleep (insomnia) - continuous noise prevents restful sleep.
2. Hypertension (high blood pressure) - noise is a major stressor.
3. Anxiety - constant noise creates mental tension and anxiety.
4. Health disorders - digestive problems, heart disease and other conditions linked to chronic noise exposure.
5. Hearing impairment - continuous exposure to very loud sounds can cause temporary or permanent damage to the hearing mechanism.

MEASURES TO CONTROL NOISE POLLUTION:
To control noise, we must control the sources of noise:
1. Technological: Silencing devices (mufflers, silencers) must be installed in aircraft engines, transport vehicles, industrial machines and home appliances.
2. Urban Planning: Noisy industries and operations must be located away from residential areas.
3. Regulations: Use of automobile horns must be minimised. "No Horn" zones near hospitals, schools and residences.
4. Personal habits: TV, music systems and loudspeakers must be run at low volumes.
5. Natural measures: Trees must be planted along roads and around buildings. Trees absorb sound and reduce noise levels.

ROLE OF SOCIETY FOR HEARING-IMPAIRED:
Children with hearing impairment are often unable to hear even in the audible range.
Society can help by:
1. Providing special education and care for hearing-impaired children.
2. Teaching sign language to enable communication.
3. Providing technological devices (hearing aids) to improve quality of life.
4. Creating an inclusive environment in schools and workplaces.
5. Improving living conditions to reduce noise and further protect hearing.
CONCLUSION: Noise pollution is a serious environmental problem with significant health impacts. Individual responsibility, government regulation and community action are all needed to control noise pollution and protect human health.

sections.label: EXERCISE 3: True or False statements:
sections.raw:
(a) Sound cannot travel in vacuum. T/F
EXERCISE ANSWER: TRUE. Sound needs a medium to travel. Vacuum has no medium, so sound cannot travel through it.

(b) The number of oscillations per second of a vibrating object is called its time period. T/F
EXERCISE ANSWER: FALSE. The number of oscillations per second is called FREQUENCY, not time period. Time period is the time taken for one complete oscillation.

(c) If the amplitude of vibration is large, sound is feeble. T/F
EXERCISE ANSWER: FALSE. If amplitude is large, the sound is LOUD (not feeble). Larger amplitude produces louder sound. Small amplitude produces feeble sound.

(d) For human ears, the audible range is 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. T/F
EXERCISE ANSWER: TRUE. The human ear can detect sounds in the frequency range of 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Sounds outside this range are inaudible to humans.

(e) The lower the frequency of vibration, the higher is the pitch. T/F
EXERCISE ANSWER: FALSE. The HIGHER the frequency, the HIGHER the pitch. Lower frequency produces lower pitch (deeper sound).

(f) Unwanted or unpleasant sound is termed as music. T/F
EXERCISE ANSWER: FALSE. Unwanted or unpleasant sound is called NOISE (not music). Music is a pleasant sound.

(g) Noise pollution may cause partial hearing impairment. T/F
EXERCISE ANSWER: TRUE. Continuous exposure to loud noise can cause temporary or permanent hearing impairment.

SOLUTION:
Given: Number of oscillations = 40, Total time = 4 seconds
Time period T = Total time / Number of oscillations = 4/40 = 0.1 second
Frequency f = 1/T = 1/0.1 = 10 Hz
OR: f = Number of oscillations / Time = 40/4 = 10 Hz
EXERCISE ANSWER: Time period = 0.1 second, Frequency = 10 Hz

MUSIC: A pleasant, regular, agreeable sound is called musical sound. It is produced by regular, periodic vibrations and pleases the ear. Examples: sound of sitar, harmonium, singing.
CAN MUSIC BECOME NOISE? Yes. Music can become noise when it is played at a very high volume. Even pleasant music, when too loud, becomes uncomfortable and irritating - that is, it becomes noise.

EXERCISE 9: List sources of noise pollution in your surroundings.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
Sources of noise pollution in our surroundings:
1. Honking of vehicles (cars, buses, motorcycles, trucks) on busy roads.
2. Sound of construction work - drilling, hammering.
3. Loudspeakers during festivals, public events.
4. Bursting of crackers during Diwali and other festivals.
5. Sound of aircraft flying overhead (near airports).
6. Machines and equipment in factories.
7. Loud music from TV, music systems and home theatres.
8. Desert coolers and air conditioners.

EXERCISE 10: Explain in what way noise pollution is harmful to humans.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
Noise pollution harms humans in the following ways:
1. LACK OF SLEEP: Continuous noise prevents peaceful sleep leading to insomnia and fatigue.
2. HYPERTENSION: Noise is a major cause of high blood pressure (hypertension).
3. ANXIETY AND STRESS: Constant exposure to noise creates mental tension and anxiety.
4. HEALTH DISORDERS: Many health problems including heart disease, digestive disorders and many other conditions are linked to chronic noise exposure.
5. HEARING IMPAIRMENT: Continuous exposure to loud sounds can cause temporary or even permanent impairment of hearing. A person near loud machinery without ear protection can lose hearing ability over time.

EXERCISE 11: Your parents are going to buy a house. They have been offered one on the roadside and another three lanes away. Which house would you suggest? Explain.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
I would strongly suggest buying the house THREE LANES AWAY FROM THE ROADSIDE.
REASONS:
1. Roadside houses are constantly exposed to noise from vehicle horns, engines and traffic - often 70-80 dB, which is near the painful level.
2. Such constant noise causes lack of sleep, hypertension, anxiety and potential hearing damage.
3. The house three lanes away has significantly lower noise levels.
4. Trees and distance naturally reduce the noise reaching the house.
5. Living away from the road also means less air pollution (vehicle fumes) and fewer accidents.
CONCLUSION: For better health, peace of mind and quality of life, the house away from the main road is the better choice.

EXERCISE 12: Sketch larynx and explain its function in your own words.
EXERCISE ANSWER:
[DIAGRAM: The larynx is a box-like structure at the upper end of the windpipe. Two vocal cords are shown stretched across it horizontally, with a narrow slit between them.]

FUNCTION OF LARYNX:
The larynx (voice box) is the sound-producing organ in humans.
It is located at the upper end of the windpipe.
Two vocal cords are stretched across the larynx with a narrow slit between them.
When the lungs force air through this slit, the vocal cords vibrate and produce sound.
Muscles can make the vocal cords tight (thin) or loose (thick), changing the pitch and quality of the voice.

EXERCISE 13: Lightning and thunder take place in the sky at the same time and at the same distance from us. Lightning is seen earlier and thunder is heard later. Can you explain why?
EXERCISE ANSWER:
Lightning and thunder occur simultaneously (at the same moment) at the same place.
However, we see lightning almost immediately and hear thunder after a delay.
This is because LIGHT and SOUND travel at very different speeds:
- Speed of light: approximately 3 x 10^8 m/s (3,00,000 km/s) - extremely fast.
- Speed of sound in air: approximately 340 m/s - much slower.
Since light travels much faster than sound, the light from lightning reaches our eyes almost instantly.
The sound (thunder) takes more time to cover the same distance.
Therefore, even though both occur at the same time and place, we see the lightning first and hear the thunder later.
This is also why we can estimate the distance of a lightning strike - by counting the seconds between the flash and the thunder.
